newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Analyst sees copper heading for fall in long term.
newsitem.headline: Analyst sees copper heading for fall in long term.

text.p: Copper is heading for another heavy fall and the market will be marked by continued volatility, metals analyst Stephen Briggs said.
Briggs, of stockbrokers E.W Balderson, said in his latest metals report that the market remained finely balanced in 1997 but mounting surpluses could be expected from next year.
"Despite numerous supply disruptions and persistent manipulation, we are as convinced as ever that copper is riding for another heavy fall," Briggs said.
Three months LME copper was bid at $2,301 a tonne around 0900 GMT on Monday -- up around $18 from Friday's close at $2,283/87.
Briggs predicted copper to reach $2,390 this year, dropping to $1,995 next year and to $1,865/tonne in 1999.
He said customers appeared to have completed restocking and predicted demand growth of 3.5 to 4.0 percent this year.
With prices rising in the wake of the Sumitomo scandal, exchange inventories had fallen again since late February.
Although strong demand and supply disruptions were part of the reason for higher prices and falling inventories, the two factors only told part of the story, Briggs said.
"Our firm belief remains that copper is uniquely subject to speculation and indeed manipulation, made possible by the market's opacity."
Briggs said even before the predicted price fall, volatility would continue.
"The industry's prolonged unusual profitability will yet be its undoing, although its steep cost curve will amply shield low cost producers," he said.
Briggs said prospects for tubing and wire and cable appeared good in developed and developing countries.

He said recent bullish analyses had relied heavily on the emergence of China as a copper destination and although there was huge demand potential, "China remains unknown, especially in a market itself murky, like copper."
